title: what larger projects/indie games is everyone attempting?
author: agarlington
selftext:
we’ve all seen the 24-hour "vibecoded" mini-projects lately (which are incredible the speed this community is moving at is insane). Arcade games and browser shooters are cool, but I’m curious about the next step. 

who is using AI not just as a gimmick, but as a core part of a **production-ready indie pipeline?** \> with **Claude Opus 4.5** handling complex logic and tools like **Meshy** and **Sloyd** maturing for 3D, or **Retro Diffusion** and **Autosprite** for pixel art—is a high-fidelity "big" game actually viable yet?

even for those outside of the VS Code area of expertise, i’m seeing teams experiment with agentic tools like **Rosebud, Dreamforge, Mako, and Ludo** to bridge the gap between "prototype" and "product." What "big" projects do you guys have in the works? Are we at the point where a small team can ship a AA-quality title using these workflows? is this something that's even viable with the current toolsets do you guys feel?

comments.author: Sleepnotdeading
comments.body:
I'm developing a script writing software to allow me to write branching narrative scripts using a combination of a node based graph editor and a screenplay style writing mode.  Character codex and scene summaries are generated by AI, and an AI writing assistant is standing by to help keep progress moving.  The markup language embedded in the two mode will (hopefully) be able to leverage hooks in Unreal engine to create the sequences and logic to stand the script up in UE.

I worked for a AAA studio and never liked their proprietary script software, and I can't use it anymore anyway, so I figured why not make my own.

comments.author: Asmaroon
comments.body:
I don't have an advanced multi-AI-software embedded pipeline as your question poses but I've been working on a roguelite tower defense idea I've had for the last 8 months or so. I have a non coding career background but have always been interested in game design (even trying to teach myself c#/ unity a few times but just not having enough freetime after work to make real progress), so I've just been powering forward with CGPT this whole time. 


The game will be like if slay the spire, bloons and vampire survivors/rogue genesia had a baby. With some inspiration from other games that I like. 


3 act structure
map is different every time for each act
Playing field is different every time
Start with 4 basic towers but have access to 20 different parts that can be placed into them to augment the tower with additional abilities and stats.
With the right combination of parts in a tower it can evolve into stronger towers who then each have their own evolutions
Characters to unlock that might influence your playstyle while you're using them who have talent trees and level up with an experience system from your runs
Account skill tree system (think poe 1) that you earn points for by just playing the game and unlocking achievements


About 2/3 of the way through but having a blast creating and testing with friends

replies.author: Other-Football72
replies.body: How hard was lip sync? that's pretty impressive

replies.author: Power-Play-PolySci
replies.body:
Using Claude code I built a pipeline tool that took the images of the characters and the text they had to speak.

First I had the tool assign Eleven labs voices to each character in the game. I then had the tool send the text and the selected voice to eleven labs via their API.

Then I sent the image and audio to lipsynch.studio to generate the lip synched video via API.  

Finally the tool collected the completed videos and saved them in the destination directory, optimized the videos and stored the URLs as metadata.

comments.author: Trashy_io
comments.body:
I’m attempting big stuff… and also actively trying not to ruin my life with it 😂

My “largest idea” is the classic trap: top-down 2D pixel zombie MMO basically if DayZ and WoW had a baby. I paused it because I realized I need reps shipping smaller games before I try to build a planet.

Release order right now:
	1.	ZomBite Arena — zombie roguelite where you are the zombie (main focus going to attempt a high quality full game probably not AA quality worthy 😅)
	2.	Bot Pit — underground bot battle pit: players build + light-program bots, fight the “house” bots, share builds/replays… eventually I want to plug different LLMs in and let them throw hands (Red Queen test but entertaining)
	3.	(Name in progress-Paused) incremental game — I'm doing all the art by free - hand and it slowed everything down, so it’s parked for now still want to finish to learn the absolute puzzle it is they call pixel art

AI as “production” for me hasn’t been magic art buttons — it’s been speed on the unsexy stuff: turning messy ideas into systems, scaffolding code, catching edge cases, and helping me keep everything editable via shared values.

My honest take on “AA with AI”: possible, but the bottleneck becomes consistency + polish + content throughput, not raw coding.
What’s the most “real” pipeline win you’ve seen so far auto-tests, asset generation, quest/content tools, or something else?

comments.author: Amazing-Treat-9293
comments.body:
I think we’re past “AI as gimmick” and into AI as leverage, but not AI as replacement. AI assist is how I’m thinking about it.

What’s working for me is treating AI like a junior dev that accelerates iteration, not a magic box. And does lots of debugging, I am constantly feeding Codex bugs. It drafts and reviews systems, explores edge cases, and helps test breadth fast—but I still own architecture, performance, and taste.

The biggest gains aren’t visuals, they’re systems density. Example: I had enemy behaviors get too good—flanking perfectly, tracking the player from behind, landing shots with inhuman consistency and speed. It was impressive…and unfun. AI sped me into that problem fast, but the real work was scaling it back: adding perception limits, reaction delays, aim noise, and difficulty curves that feel fair. That human tuning/testing is still essential.

Content-wise, generative art is great for scaffolding, but it’s trashy. But still, I can prototype 10 enemy archetypes before committing to 2 that get polished. Agentic tools help the most when tasks are tightly scoped; open-ended “build my game” still breaks down. Gotta be precise in your mechanical descriptions and math.

So can small teams ship AA-quality games right now?
	•	AA scope: yes
	•	AA polish: only with humans in the loop
	•	Best fit: systems-heavy games over asset-heavy ones

AI can make games deeper and more intgrates, but you’re going to have to supply the vision. Curious what others are seeing once projects move past the demo phase.

replies.author: agarlington
replies.body: That best fit is a good quote to work off philosophically; use AI for systems rather than assets. Hmm.

comments.author: HONGSHIreddit
comments.body:
Hey I'm a new solo indie dev that's started not so long ago but I've been using Bezi for my workflow and I have to say it's been a game changer for me (pun intended).

I've always had trouble with coding and I've been stuck in tutorial hell for the longest time which prevented me from finishing any project. Ever since I found out about Bezi, I've actually been able to finish a project although it was for a game jam for the first time. Now I'm currently working on a co-op multiplayer horror game through vibe coding, I was able to create my core gameplay loop and I was also able to integrate the Steam API so I can connect with players through Steam.

These are things I probably couldn't have done by myself unless I put years of learning mainly because following tutorials does not help in the long run. Not only am I vibe coding all the functions for my game, I'm actively learning as if I have a personal tutor who tells me why certain things work, why this code should work for what I'm looking for, and if certain things don't work, it gets me to think about other ways to engineer the function. 

There is also a learning curve on how to use the application but once you get over that hurdle I think it's smooth sailing. From my experience, a lot of newcomers seem to have a negative experience because it doesn't work the way they want out of the box like other AI tools (chatgpt, claude etc). The fact that you have to set it up to your workflow preference is what I think makes it a more powerful tool and the fact that it uses all the assets in your project as reference so it doesn't just create random code is amazing.

comments.author: SproutsJeremy
comments.body:
> What "big" projects do you guys have in the works?

I’m working on a text based open world lifesim/rpg. 

Basically all of Skyrim + Sims 4 features put into a text game format with background images for thousands of locations and character visuals for tens of thousands of characters. Everything is pre generated, no gen AI in final product. (so it’s completely playable offline, no gen AI needed)

Without gen AI, it probably would’ve taken another year or two just for the code alone, not including all the content it comes with. 

> is a high-fidelity "big" game actually viable yet? (With AI as a core part og a production ready indie pipeline) 

Yeah, but you may still need to know code depending on how far you want to go with it. But you can get pretty far knowing 0 code. It also depends on the engine you’re using. The more well known it is, the better your code comes out.

> Are we at the point where a small team can ship a AA-quality title using these workflows? 

Yeah, for sure. Though it depends on the stuff I mention above. 

> is this something that's even viable with the current toolsets do you guys feel?

Same as the above

comments.author: gbradburn
comments.body:
I've been using Bezi for my most recent projects. The biggest one by far was a social studies game I made for Legends of Learning. I couldn't use a lot of commercial assets because the project contraints were so strict (e.g. uncompressed build-size must be less than 30MB and it has to run well on low-end Chromebooks).   
That mean writing lean & mean systems from scratch and Bezi really made that possible given the 10 week window I had to deliver the game.   
Some of systems I developed for the game were:  
A dialogue system, task/quest system, influence system, poor-man's alternative to navmesh navigation. This included custom editors to the dialogue trees and tasks/objectives/quests.
